title: Fukanzazengi Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the picture book Moody Cow Meditates, in which a grandfather settles a jar of sparkles to quiet a boy's angry day, and then returns to the opening of Dogen's Fukanzazengi. Nomon dwells on the turn of "and yet," where a slight discrepancy, a hundredth of a fine hair, lets liking and disliking arise. Nomon sets Norman Fischer's objection to the phrase "pride of understanding" beside the Tanahashi and Levitt translation, which sends practice back to the body. Nomon tells of Master Ruiyan calling "Master!" to himself and answering "Yes?" each day, then closes with the backward step that turns the light inward.
topics: Soto Zen teachings on mindfulness and meditation
Dogen's writing on Chinese Buddhist canon
jar of water and sparkles analogy
Soto Zen emphasis on honoring ancestors

sentences.text: Downshifting, isn't it?
To just sit quietly together.
I was thinking, we always used to have little inexpensive Japanese cars, really simple cars with manual transmissions.
When you were cruising down the freeway in fifth gear, you knew it.
You could really hear the engine.
Did you have a car like that?
Now we have a car where you can't even tell what it's doing.
It just goes.
And I was thinking, that's how we are a lot of the time in our life, right?
When you're cruising down the freeway all day on a road trip or something, you get used to it.
So maybe these structures that we inherited are really just support, and just: what is this vehicle?
So I have a short subject for you first.
Moody Cow Meditates.
*My name is Moody Cow.
It used to be Peter, but now it's Moody Cow.
It all started one stupid rotten day when everything went wrong.
First I had a bad dream.* Hopefully you'll be able to see, okay?
*A very bad dream, which involved a giant three-eyed alien.* You can substitute career anxiety or whatever you want.
*What a rotten way to wake up.*
*I wanted to find my mind and tell her about the giant three-eyed alien, but I couldn't find her anywhere.
And so I admit I was in a bad mood to begin with, and then I couldn't find my skateboard.
Turns out my sister had borrowed it.
"Daisy, stop drawing on my skateboard!"
Okay, maybe I overreacted when I pulled her tail, but it was a brand new skateboard.
And so then Daisy had to get me back by tripping me on the stairs.
What a monster.
Mad, so mad that I cut her doll's hair off on purpose.
Of course I got in trouble for that, which made me miss the bus.*
*I had to ride my bike all the way to school in the snow.
That made me really mad.
On the way home from school, I hit a snowbank and I scraped my knee and there was blood everywhere.
And the rest of the way, I couldn't stop thinking about how my rotten day was really Daisy's fault.
She put me in a bad mood by drawing on my new skateboard.
Maybe it was the giant three-eyed alien's fault for giving me bad dreams, whatever.
I was so mad I couldn't see straight.
And then when I turned into our driveway, I crashed into my dad's truck.*
You can understand that with a bloody knee and a banged up nose, I was madder than ever.
Super mad.* What about his ears now?
*So then I did something crazy.
I picked up my baseball and I threw it right through the window.
On purpose.
Unfortunately, my mom saw the whole thing.
"What on earth do you think you're doing?" she yelled.
"Have you lost your mind?"
She came outside and took one look at my super mad rotten day face.*
*I guess she did feel sorry for me.
"Aw.
Are you a little moody cow?"
Of course my sister Daisy heard that.* In the background, she and her friends are yelling, "Moody cow, moody cow, moody moody, moody cow."
*She started shouting, "Moody cow, Peter is a moody cow."
The next thing I knew, all the kids in the neighborhood joined in.
"We need Grandfather," Mom said.*
*I picked up the phone.
Pretty soon, my grandfather was sitting in the sunroom on a meditation cushion.
I got to sit on one too.* Mmm.
*"I hear they're calling you Moody Cow," Grandfather said and smiled.
I couldn't help smiling back a little.
I guess Moody Cow was kind of a funny name.* So here's Grandfather Cow.
*"See this?"
"Yes," as he pointed to a jar of water.
"This is your mind.
And these," he held out a little dish of sparkles, "are your angry thoughts."
"That," I said, "is a jar of water.
Those are Daisy's fairy dust sparkles."
"Come on, Moody Cow, work with me here.
Now, what we're going to do is put a pinch of sparkles into the water for every angry thought that you have.
Then we're going to sit here until they all settle down to the bottom.*
*By the time the water is clear again, your anger will have settled down too."
"That won't work," I said.
"Let's just see," he said.
So I took a pinch of sparkles and dropped it in the water.
"What angry thought is that?"
Grandfather asked.
"That's the three-eyed alien who tried to gobble me last night."
"Oh, I see.*
*Rotten way to start the day.
Okay, what else?"
I took another pinch for the next angry thought.
"This is me having to clean the toilet for a whole month for breaking the window.
I hate cleaning the toilet."
"Me too.
What else?"
I put in one more pinch of sparkles and said,*
*"This is Daisy drawing on my brand new skateboard with a marker."
"Oh dear, would she do that?"
Grandfather sighed.
"Okay, what else?"
"This pinch is for when I miss the bus and I ride my bike to school in the snow."
"You can ride a bike through snow?"
Grandfather asked.
"I have good tires."*
*"Anything else?"
"On my way home I scraped my knee.
I was so mad I crashed into Dad's truck.
I think I broke my nose."
"Ouch!"
Grandfather said.
"That must have hurt."
"It did.
Then I picked up my baseball and threw it through the window on purpose."*
*"Oh, maybe you should do a double pinch for that one.
I guess you did have a Moody Cow day."
"I sure did."
"Is that all?"
Grandfather asked.
"Yeah, but it's a lot."
"It sure is," he said.
Then Grandfather put the lid on the jar and shook it up really good.*
*"This jar is your mind right now," he said.
"Angry thoughts bouncing around all over the place.
Now let's see what happens when we let your angry thoughts settle down," Grandfather said, putting the mind jar right in front of me.
"Just sit quietly and see what happens."
I sat up real straight.
Then I got to ring the gong.
Bong!*
*I sat watching all my angry thoughts swirl around like crazy in the jar.
A few thoughts slowed down and sank to the bottom.
Then a few more and then a few more.
It was so still I could hear my heart beating.
It was so quiet I could hear my breath.
Going in and out.
In and out.
I felt a ray of golden sunshine coming through the window.*
*It warmed my back.
Started to melt away the last bit of anger.* [unclear: "In the meditation, you"] *leaned over to whisper in my ear.
"Okay," he said.
"This part's important.
Don't move until you can't hear the sound of the gong anymore."
So I cocked my head and listened very carefully.
Bong!*
*The ringing got softer and softer and softer.
Until I couldn't hear it at all.
Grandfather smiled and held up the jar.
"Well, look at this.
All the sparkles have settled down," he said.
"My angry thoughts have too," I said.
"I mean, I guess if I think about it I could get mad again."
"That's probably true," he said.*
*"But we have to work pretty hard to settle them down.
Let's not stir them up again."
And I laughed for the first time that day.
"Oh, that thing is cool," I said.
"Can I keep it?"
"Sure," said Grandfather.
He smiled and handed me the jar and the dish of sparkles.
A few minutes each day helps keep Moody Cow away.*
*I laughed again.
"Thanks, Grandfather.
Can we do this again tomorrow?"
"Of course.
Let's try to do this together every day."
I went to my room and put the mind jar by my bed, just in case the three-eyed alien ever comes back.
And now it's been two whole weeks and I haven't had one moody cow day.
I've decided to keep the name anyway.
I kind of like it.*
I don't know if you can see, but he's crossing Peter off on his door and writing moody cow instead.
That's my favorite part, actually.
You understand.
The end.
There are actually directions for how to create your own moody cow jar in the back.
That would be the worst idea.
Anyway, I just bring that up because it's worth remembering that this practice has a very simple root to it.
And we are so complicated, and so smart in looking for complicated solutions to our complicated problems.
Notably, Grandfather did not help Peter deconstruct his day, or figure out how to solve his problems with his sister, or have a long conversation about the contents of his mind, right?
They just let it settle, which is essentially what we're trying to do in Zazen.
So I thought for the rest of the talk I'd talk a little bit more about Fukanzazengi, which we chanted this morning.
If you weren't here a couple of weeks ago, we started talking about Fukanzazengi then.
So I'll just give you a brief summary of how I spent a whole talk on, like, the first paragraph.
But that's how it goes.
This is Dogen's text about Zazen, and studying it this time, I realize it was really a mission statement.
He wrote this pretty soon after he came back from his adventures in China and established his first very small monastery on the outskirts of Kyoto.
I think he wrote it to clarify what he was trying to do, for himself and for the others.
And he pretty much stuck to this for the rest of his life in various ways, exploring the subtleties and the nuances of the ways that we understand the world or don't.
But essentially, his advice is like Grandfather cow's.
So the opening part, which we chanted this morning: does that sound familiar?
Remember chanting this?
A long time ago.
*The way is basically perfect and all-pervading.
How could it be contingent on practice and realization?
The Dharma vehicle is free and untrammeled.
What need is there for concentrated effort?
Indeed, the whole body is far beyond the world's dust.
Who could believe in a means to brush it clean?
It is never apart from one, right where one is.
What is the use of going off here and there to practice?*
So the opening is focused on the settled jar that we already have.
I was reflecting in the last talk that it's a strange opening in a way, from our conventional point of view.
If we were trying to sell meditation practice, we probably wouldn't start with this whole section about how you're basically perfect already and there's no need to practice.
We would probably instead explore the problems.
We'd focus on the sparkles, right?
You've got all these sparkles and you need Zazen.
This is really going to help you.
But actually, Dogen's focused on the water.
He's focused on the clarity.
The sparkles, you can see, are so small that we can feel the whole jar.
Not to overuse the moody cow metaphor too much.
But another way to look at this is to deeply recognize what's right with you.
So much is right with us.
Just the fact that we're even alive is unbelievably right.
It's unbelievably awakening already.
How could that even be, that we're alive and in this room together in this space, with our pains and our this's and that's and our emotions and our sparkles?
And yet, here we are.
So that's how he opens it.
But then there's a turning word right after that.
This is the part I want to focus on today, because this is where sesshin is so useful to us.
Then he says, "and yet."
And yet.
Which is essentially where the whole of Buddhism is, I've seen, and especially Zen.
It's like Issa, the Japanese Buddhist poet.
Do you know Issa?
Seventeenth century, maybe.
He has a famous poem that uses that same phrase, and Dogen's using the same characters: and yet.
In Issa's case, a very subtle practitioner, and he must have been a lay practitioner because he had kids, his daughter dies young.
He supposedly wrote this poem right after the funeral at the grave site.
Hopefully I can remember it and write it down.
Something like, *this lotus world is a perfect lotus world, and yet.* The Japanese culture maybe really appreciates that sense of beauty and sadness together.
We want beauty in good times, like, yee-haw.
So it's a somewhat different sensibility.
So Dogen also says, and yet, things are perfect.
There's this clear jar, and yet.
He says:
*If there's the slightest discrepancy, the way is as distant as heaven from earth.
If the least like or dislike arises, the mind is lost in confusion.*
So anyway, here we are this morning in our version of this perfect Zen monastic life.
Did any likes or dislikes arise so far?
Oh, really?
The mind is lost in confusion.
But he says it's a slight discrepancy.
There's a slight sense of being off in some way.
And here we're into preferences, right?
Here we're into personality.
Here we're into our self-reference.
What do I like?
What do I dislike?
You can't really have liking and disliking without an I.
Otherwise, it would just be sparkles.
It would just be dust.
The I is what gives it weight and strength and power.
And of course, when we're upset about something, not getting what we want or getting what we don't want, do we focus on that part of it?
No.
We focus on the object.
We focus on the like or dislike, not on the I that's generating the whole thing.
This may, in Dogen's case, also be a reference to the famous poem of Senkan called Faith and Mind.
We've talked about it before, which has this famous first line, right?
*The great way is not difficult.
Just set aside picking and choosing.* And so the sesshin, the container, is in a way an experimental lab for noticing picking and choosing and setting it aside.
If the container's strong, you don't have any choice.
If the bell rang, you have to sit.
If they pass the bowl, you have to eat that, you know?
Not what you wanted.
This.
So that's a way of working with this very experientially and very directly.
And then this phrase about the slightest discrepancy.
There's so many.
I'm going to sound really smarter than I am here because there's so many great resources online.
So I found online a resource by one of the famous English translators of Dogen, Mike Cross.
He's a guy from the UK.
And he created this website about Fukanzazengi where he shows each character, and it's actually pictures from a text written in Dogen's hand.
Each character and what it means.

And so you can see there's places where the English translation seems pretty close to what the characters are saying, and there's places where it's just really hard to make that jump between a series of ideographs and English grammar and thinking.
But anyway, the characters for this slight discrepancy are two characters.
The first means a fine hair.
A fine hair.
And the second character means a hundredth.
So that's how far off we are from the Great Way.
Not very far.
A hundredth of a fine hair.
Not even a thick hair.
A fine hair.
So that's like good news and bad news, right?
The good news is the slightest shift in this habitual self-generated pattern of life, where we're isolated and liking and disliking and separated and angry: the slightest shift in that is huge.
It goes right back into the Buddha way.
So that's the good news.
But the bad news is, then you're going to be off again, right?
The slightest shift.
And one way to look at being human is we're always a hair's breadth off.
Is that something we have to fix?
Or is it just the nature of our living that we can work with and practice with?
It's not so clear.
He's not saying fix the discrepancy exactly either.
He's recognizing this reality.
A good way to study this slight discrepancy is, well, there's many good ways, right?
All strong emotions are good ways.
But the one I think of is righteousness.
When we think we're right, then we're not.
That's the discrepancy.
That's what oozes out of that tiny little gap that's a thousandth of a fine hair's width: I'm right, you're wrong.
Then Dogen goes on to say:

*Suppose one gains pride of understanding and inflates one's own enlightenment, glimpsing the wisdom that runs through all things, attaining the way and clarifying the mind, raising an aspiration to escalate the very sky.
One is making the initial partial excursions about the frontiers, but is still somewhat deficient in the vital way of total emancipation.*
So that's a very dense paragraph.
Let's read it again.
*Suppose one gains pride of understanding and inflates one's own enlightenment, glimpsing the wisdom that runs through all things, attaining the way and clarifying the mind.*
So this all sounds good, you know?
Clarifying, attaining, understanding, raising an aspiration to escalate the very sky.
So we're really excited.
We're feeling better.
We're feeling in harmony with something.
*At that point, one is making the initial partial excursions about the frontiers, but is still somewhat deficient in the vital way of total emancipation.*
So some kind of pointer here to a few things.
And the obvious one, of course, is pride, which naturally arises.
But the other is the depth and endlessness of this journey of exploration.
It's sort of both affirming of something.
There is a sense here that you can understand something more clearly about your life.
You can have a connection with wisdom.
You can clarify the mind.
You can be very expansive, like you're ready to escalate the very sky, kind of funny English expression.
And yet, that's incomplete.
That's partial.
Please look again.
Please humbly examine your understanding.

One of the great things I've been thinking about, and we talked about this today, too, what's great about chanting a text over and over again, whether you've studied it or talked about it or even thought about it, particularly outside of the service, is that some of the phrases just get into your mind in some subconscious way, sort of enter into this storehouse of consciousness.
And sometimes they pop up just when you need them.
You could chant this phrase about pride a million times, and that's nice, yeah.
But then at some point the conditions might be right for it just to leap forth.
And you say, oh my gosh, I was feeling so right and so good about dharma.
*I suppose one gets pride of understanding*, but it just all comes.
So that's a wonderful aspect of our liturgical practice.
And actually this particular phrase was very important to me because summer came very strongly to mind, the whole thing.
The thing about pride now is the whole thing just started cycling through my mind.
It was very helpful.
Because all of this is not fodder for beating ourselves up.
We're never going to be good enough.
Dogen says so.
We're always going to be a little bit off.
We're going to be pride.
We're going to be partial.
Whoa.
I quit now.
That's not at all what he's doing.
He's just trying to encourage us to be humble and keep practicing.
So I really appreciate this phrase, but actually I was reading a talk that Norman Fischer gave on Fukanzazengi, and he's critical of this phrase.
So I want to read you what he says.
You get another point of view.
Norman said about this particular phrase:
*I think that this translation, in my opinion, in my understanding of the text, is a little bit misleading.
Because our translator didn't entirely appreciate Dogen's point here.
Using words like pride of understanding and inflates one's enlightenment makes it sound as if this is somebody whose enlightenment is imperfect and not quite right.
This makes it sound like a tainted experience of enlightenment.
But I don't think Dogen means that.

The way I would translate it is that I would take those words out and I would say, suppose one gains understanding and enlightenment and sees the wisdom that runs through all things and attains the way and clarifies the mind and raising an aspiration that goes up to the skies.
Suppose that happens.
Suppose our fantasies about how we're going to become Buddhas, our fantasies about how we're going to become Buddhas and everything, all comes true.
Suppose the end of this very retreat, we all walk out and say, I'm enlightened.
It's unbelievable.
This is great.
It happened.
Wouldn't that be great?*
So Norman's bringing up the side of this which is important to bring up too: that any sort of conception we have of practice is limited by its conceptual nature.
And the sense that we have that we're somehow broken and incomplete and there's some other enlightenment over there is a very rigid, dualistic notion.
And this was really the theme that Dogen explored all his life.
How can it be that there's some sense of complete awakening, Buddha nature?
Things are just as they are, just right.
How can that be true?
And at the same time, how can it be true that we are prideful?
We are confused.
We're upset.
We are angry.
We are lashing out.
How can these two things coexist?
And so we have to look at both of them in this particular passage.
Norman's more interested in this sort of emptiness side of this, the complete side of this.
There's no enlightenment for you to get.
There's nothing for you to attain.
And the minute you think so, you're putting yourself on a little hamster wheel.
You're just making this into another project.
You're never going to get to the end of that.

But actually I looked at the character by character translation, and Norman's wish is kind of wishful thinking actually, because Dogen very clearly has the characters for pride, understanding, and enlightenment in there.
So I have to take my teacher to task a little bit.
Sometimes we want the text to say what we want it to say.
And that's fine too.
There's no right and wrong teaching here.
It's just each of us trying to bring up our understanding of how are things really, how do we work with this life the way it actually is.
So there's another translation, a good recent translation.
These are reliable translators, Kazoaki Tenohashi and Peter Levitt.
They translated this passage.
*You could be proud of your understanding and have abundant realization or acquire outstanding wisdom and attain the way by clarifying the mind.
Still, if you're wandering about in your head, you miss the vital path of letting your body leap.*
So that's interesting, very different.
*You could be proud of your understanding and have abundant realization,*
so that's similar,
*or acquire outstanding wisdom and attain the way by clarifying the mind.
Still, if you're only wandering about in your head, you may miss the vital path of letting your body leap.*
And so the actual characters do talk about the body very directly, so it's important parts to bring up.
And Dogen from the beginning was saying, this is an embodied practice.
That's really an easy one for us to miss or forget and have to rediscover and relearn: this is not a mental exercise.
Our self-concept is so embedded in thinking.
It's so easy for us to think, okay, I just need better thoughts.
If I could just outthink my thinking and think about my problems in a better way, I'd be happy, or whatever it is we want.
But actually, the practice is not a thought practice.
Thoughts are just one aspect of experience, one aspect of reality.
And it might be time for us to take some of our identification and energy and withdraw that from the realm of thought, to not give thought so much chutzpah in our life.
And what are the obvious alternatives?
Sensations.
And the Buddhists didn't really talk about emotions as separate from thinking, but I think it's helpful for us to think about emotion kind of as a tone, as a feeling.
So not the contents of why we're this way or why we're that way or why she should have done it this way or why they shouldn't have served us yogurt.
Don't they know I'm not dairy?
But the actual feeling: oh, irritation.
There's some feeling with the whole body.
I can't even put a word on it, because once you put a word on it, you're already a little bit in the realm of thought.

So Dogen here in our text, right away emphasizing in this text from the very beginning, that pride and that disconnection, that possible sort of misuse in a way of understanding, may have to do with leaving your body, with forgetting your body.
Please return to the body.
And he had a famous phrase, his sort of phrase for awakening: dropping away body and mind.
Dropping away body and mind.
So body and mind in some way in harmony, and in some way just released from the conceptual world completely.
And another thing in this little passage is the character Ki is there, like in Aikido, the character for energy.
So Dogen recommending that we bring up some energy in our practice.
It requires effort.
And this whole passage about pride and understanding and how you are working with this, in a way it has sort of an element of just be alert, be awake.
And it makes me think, don't fool yourself into thinking you are somebody who can possess something or who doesn't possess something, which is kind of the side Norman's bringing up.
Don't think you're not enlightened.
And don't think you are enlightened.
And it made me think of a wonderful koan, so just mention a koan as an aside.
And who knows if Dogen was trying to reference this or not.
The other thing about Dogen's writing is it's just outrageously dense with references, most of which we will probably never know.

Somehow Dogen, in addition to having such a deep feeling for practice, embodied practice, and this sort of two-sided koan of the perfection of our life and the need to practice, in addition to that, the guy was a real brainiac.
Somehow he went to China for around three years, we don't know exactly how long he was in China, and just absorbed this enormous Chinese Buddhist canon.
And the Chinese Buddhist canon itself completely absorbed thousands of years of Chinese literary history, and somehow Dogen just sucked that up.
I don't know how he did it.
We don't really know what he brought back, but he certainly brought back some texts.
But the level of stuff that he references in Chinese Chan and Chinese literary history is just unbelievable.
Now we have to study for decades just to get a sense of what he's talking about.
Anyway, who knows if he's referencing this story, but it's a good story.
Every day, Master Ruyuan, Ruyuan, some of these names are hard, every day Master Ruyuan would call to himself, "Master, Master!"
And every day he would respond, "Yes?"
And then he would say, "Be awake, be alert!
From now on, don't be fooled by anything!"
"Okay, I won't be!"
So every day, this was his daily practice, to call to himself, to call himself forth, "Master, Master."
You could use your own name: "Tim, Tim!"
And answer yourself, "Yes?"
And you can see the value of that right away, right?
There's a way that you're not home sometimes, right?
So show up.
Show up in your life.
Call yourself, and knock on your own door.
Show up in your life: "Yes?"
And remind yourself, be awake, be alert.
You'll notice, what's happening now?
What are you feeling now?
"Yes, I'll be alert!"
And remind yourself, don't be fooled!
So just like Moody Cow, don't be fooled by your [unclear: "violent sparkles"].
Don't be fooled by your pride of understanding.
Don't be fooled by thinking you're broken in some way.
"Okay, I won't be."
Repeat.
So Dogen goes on.
*Need I mention the Buddha, who was possessed of inborn knowledge?
The influence of his six years of upright sitting is noticeable still, or Bodhidharma's transmission of the mind seal.
The fame of his nine years of well-sitting is celebrated to this day.*
Now to us, this reads like examples, encouraging us to sort of do something.
Need I mention such-and-so example?
But I don't think Dogen meant these as examples.
Of course we see them as examples right away: we don't quite measure up, right?
Actually, I think what he's doing is reminding us of ancestors.
These are the two most important ancestors in our mythopoetic Zen world, Buddha and Bodhidharma.
In the very first paragraph, which I got into last time, there was a reference to another ancestor, Huineng, also important.
Last summer some of us got to go to Japan.
Norman and some of us went to Japan.
Actually, Norman didn't want us to go there to learn ceremonies or how to do it right or anything like that.
He didn't really care if we learned any Japanese.
He wanted us to go to Japan to have some feeling, some experiential sense of the importance of ancestors in the practice.
Maybe one day we'll organize another trip, a Bellingham Northwest trip, because I'd really like you to have this experience too.
Who knows what you'll experience.

But we did have some small experience of something that's really baked into the culture and lived day by day in Japan, and probably throughout Asia: the sense of ancestors not being in the past, and not being some distant thing that we're independent of and now asserting ourselves in our independence and the primacy of our generation.
It's more a sense of our work being to uphold and honor the ancestors, and that our honor and our support is to be part of a sort of matrix.
They know historically that these people are long dead, if they ever lived at all.
But at the same time there's a feeling that's beyond that.
This exists actually here too, in the native cultures that lived here for so many thousands of years.
Jeff and Kate hangs around there too.
He has some sense of this, and often we bring up ancestors.
He always has the same sort of sense of it, and if you go, you can easily access this through him.
They have a sweat lodge every Thursday night.
During the sweat lodge they say this phrase over and over again, "all my relations, all my relations," thinking about the ancestors.
They have some feeling that the spot of dirt they're sitting on has had presence from their ancestors for thousands of years.
It's the same in Asia, and it's the same with your birth family ancestors and your spiritual ancestors.
They're really right here with you.
Without this sense of ancestors there really is no practice.
There's a deep sense of connection.
I think little by little, and it's going to take us some hundreds of years, this generation will just get the ball rolling, maybe.
We'll start to have that feeling in our practice that it's not about me and now.
That's how we think, right?
We have to admit it: we think it's about me and now.
So the sense here of bringing up Buddha and Bodhidharma is, remember, this is much, much bigger than that.
It transcends time.
It transcends the personal.
It transcends this idea that you think you're separate.

One textual note that's really interesting, and I'm grateful to Mike Cross for this: the characters he used for Buddha in this passage were the usual two characters for Shakyamuni, which means sage of the Shakyamuni clan.
They have lots of names for Buddha, and that's one of them.
But then he had two more characters for Roshi, like "old teacher," an honorific in Japan.
